recipe.history:
Kale — Brassica oleracea var. acephala — is one of the oldest cultivated brassicas in existence, with evidence of its consumption stretching back over two thousand years to ancient Rome and Greece, where it was a common food crop grown throughout the Mediterranean basin. Unlike cabbage, kale does not form a head, which may have made it more adaptable to diverse climates, and it spread northward through Europe with remarkable efficiency. In Scotland and the Netherlands it became a staple winter vegetable — the Scots called a basic meal of kale and other greens simply 'kale,' the word becoming synonymous with dinner itself. In Portugal, caldo verde, a simple kale and potato soup, remains the country's most beloved comfort food. Across the African diaspora, particularly in the American South, leafy greens in the kale family cooked low and slow with smoked pork became a cornerstone of soul food — a tradition of extraordinary depth and cultural significance.

Kale's recent American cultural history is a story of spectacular reinvention. For decades it was considered peasant food, cattle feed, or at best a garnish on buffet tables — purely decorative, mostly ignored. Then, in the early 2010s, it became the defining superfood of a wellness movement, appearing in smoothies, grain bowls, and salads at every health-conscious restaurant in the country. The kale Caesar salad became ubiquitous. Kale chips appeared in every natural foods store. Burger culture embraced kale in two forms: as a raw topping (massaged with lemon and salt to soften its tough fibers) and as a cooked topping (sautéed or wilted with garlic and olive oil until it collapses into something silky and deeply savory). The latter is the more interesting application, particularly when paired with sharp cheese and smoky bacon.

I resisted kale for years with the stubborn pride of someone who had decided to have an opinion before tasting the thing. I had been burned by too many limp, fibrous kale salads dressed in too much lemon and served with too much self-congratulation. Then a friend made me a bowl of kale braised low and slow with chicken stock, garlic, and a strip of smoked bacon until every trace of toughness was gone and the leaves had become something tender and rich and smoky, and I reconsidered everything. I had been cooking kale wrong. Most people are. The vegetable is not delicate — it wants heat, it wants fat, it wants time, and when it gets all three it becomes one of the most satisfying things in the plant kingdom.

A medium-rare patty at 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit is what elevates this burger from interesting to extraordinary. The sautéed kale in this recipe is rich and garlicky and slightly bitter — it needs the juicy, fatty, yielding quality of properly cooked medium-rare beef to anchor it. An overcooked patty would make the kale seem even more aggressive, throwing the burger out of balance. But medium-rare beef is generous — it meets the kale halfway, its rendered fat mingling with the olive oil and garlic from the greens, creating a single unified richness in every bite. Cook it right. The kale and your guests both deserve it.
ingredients: 300g Tuscan (lacinato/dinosaur) kale, stems removed, leaves torn
instructions: 1. Make the buns: Combine warm milk, yeast, and sugar in a stand mixer bowl. Let sit 5 minutes until foamy. Add flour, salt, egg, and butter. Knead on medium 8 minutes. Transfer to oiled bowl, cover, rise 1 to 1.5 hours. Shape into 4 balls, proof 45 minutes. Brush with egg wash. Bake at 375°F (190°C) 16 to 18 minutes until golden. Cool on a rack.

2. Make the smoky aioli: Whisk egg yolks, vinegar, smoked paprika, chipotle powder, grated garlic, honey, and salt in a bowl. Drizzle in oil in a very slow, thin stream while whisking constantly until fully emulsified and thick. Taste and adjust heat and salt. Refrigerate.

3. Cook the bacon: Lay bacon strips in a cold skillet. Turn heat to medium. Cook, turning occasionally, until deeply crispy, about 8 to 10 minutes. Transfer to a paper-towel-lined plate. Reserve 1 tablespoon of bacon fat in the skillet.

4. Sauté the kale: Add olive oil to the skillet with the reserved bacon fat over medium-high heat. Add garlic slices and red pepper flakes. Cook 60 seconds until golden. Add torn kale leaves and toss to coat. Add stock. Cook, stirring frequently, 5 to 6 minutes until kale is completely wilted and tender and stock has evaporated. Add red wine vinegar and salt. Toss and remove from heat.

5. Prepare the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 equal portions (about 175g each). Form each into a patty 4 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick. Make a thumb dimple in the center. Season both sides with salt, pepper, and smoked paprika just before cooking.

6. Cook the patties: Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Sear patties 3 minutes undisturbed. Flip and place a slice of sharp cheddar on each. Cook 2 to 2.5 minutes more until the internal temperature reads 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C). Remove and rest 3 minutes.
7. Toast bun cut sides in the skillet fat over medium heat until golden, about 90 seconds.

8. Assemble: Spread smoky aioli generously on both cut bun surfaces. Set the rested patty with melted cheddar on the bottom bun. Lay a strip of crispy bacon over the patty. Pile a generous mound of garlicky sautéed kale on top of the bacon. Finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt. Cap with the top bun and serve immediately.
